item.title: Hierarchical neural circuit theory of normalization and inter-areal communication.
item.description:
eLife
The primate brain exhibits a hierarchical, modular architecture with conserved microcircuits executing canonical computations across reciprocally connected cortical areas. We present a hierarchical neural circuit theory with feedback connections that dynamically implements divisive normalization across its hierarchy. In a two-stage instantiation (V1 ↔ V2), increasing feedback from V2 to V1 amplifies responses in both areas. We analytically derive power spectra (V1) and coherence spectra (V1-V2) as functions of frequency (f) and compare them with experimental observations: peaks in both spectra shift to higher frequencies with increased stimulus contrast, and power decays as 1/f4 at high frequencies. The closed-form spectra are validated against direct stochastic simulation of the full nonlinear circuit across contrasts. The theory further predicts distinctive spectral signatures of feedback and input gain modulation. Crucially, the theory offers a unified view of inter-areal communication, defined as the ability to linearly predict neural activity in one brain area from neural activity in another, with emergent features consistent with empirical observations of both communication subspaces and inter-areal coherence. It admits a low-dimensional communication subspace, where inter-areal communication is lower-dimensional than within-area communication. It further predicts that: (1) increasing feedback strength enhances inter-areal communication and diminishes within-area communication, without altering the subspace dimensionality; (2) communication is strongest, and the subspace dimensionality lowest, at the frequencies at which V1-V2 coherence peaks; (3) normalization reduces the subspace dimensionality. Finally, a three-area (V1 ↔ V4 and V1 ↔ V5) instantiation of the theory demonstrates that differential feedback from higher to lower cortical areas dictates their dynamic functional connectivity. Altogether, our theory provides a robust and analytically tractable framework for generating experimentally testable predictions about normalization, inter-areal communication, and functional connectivity.

item.title: Transferring active inference to newly encountered prism-shifted environments.
item.description:
Communications biology
Rapid adaptability to sudden changes in environmental contingencies is a hallmark of biological intelligence. However, how animals flexibly adapt to novel environments remains largely unclear. To investigate the brain's generalizability, this work focuses on prism adaptation, a classical visuomotor phenomenon reflecting rapid recalibration of perception-action coupling. Modeling is conducted based on canonical neural networks that instantiate active inference at the circuit level. Namely, we develop canonical neural networks equipped with multiple policy matrices in parallel, enabling the reuse of previously acquired sensorimotor knowledge. We demonstrate that the proposed model recapitulates key features of prism adaptation in an arm-reaching task, including rapid error reduction and after-effects following prism removal. Networks employing policies pretrained for different target positions adapt substantially faster than naive networks that relearn policies from scratch. These results suggest a biologically plausible mechanism by which neural circuits flexibly reuse prior knowledge to support rapid adaptation.

item.title: Causal role of human hippocampus in relational structure learning and inference.
item.description:
Nature human behaviour
When meeting new individuals or known individuals in new circumstances, we intuitively map out their relationships-not merely through direct experience, but by inferring new connections on the basis of prior relational knowledge. How such relational knowledge is represented and used in the brain remains a long-standing question in cognitive neuroscience. Here, using a behavioural task and computational modelling, we show that participants (N = 36) leveraged existing knowledge of relational structures to infer new relationships, facilitating adaptation in changing environments. Whole-brain neuroimaging identified consistent representations of relational structure in the hippocampus. To investigate the causal link between hippocampal representations and inference, we used neural network simulations to predict the behavioural effects of disrupting such representations. Consistent with this prediction, transcranial ultrasound stimulation of the human hippocampus (N = 20), transiently modulating its activity, disrupted structure-based inference (P < 0.001, Cohen's d = -0.89, 95% confidence interval -1.41 to -0.36), providing empirical evidence for a causal role of hippocampus in relational-structure learning and structure-based inference.

item.title: From Variability to Synchrony: Non-linear Development of Auditory Neural Responses During the First Year of Life.
item.description:
NeuroImage
In humans, the first year of life is characterized by rapid developmental changes, including substantial brain maturation. As a result, neural responses to auditory stimuli undergo marked changes during this period. In this study, we followed 69 infants across their first year of life and recorded high-density electroencephalography (hdEEG) at 2 weeks, 6 months, and 12 months postpartum. Infants were presented with pure beep tones to examine the development of neural responses to auditory stimulation. We analyzed event-related potentials (ERPs), inter-trial phase coherence (ITPC), and event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP) responses to the beep tones and controlled for arousal state during stimulus presentation. We found that with increasing age, neural responses became more pronounced and showed reduced trial-to-trial variability. Phase synchronization increased from 2 weeks to later developmental stages in a broad low-frequency range (0.5 Hz to 13.6 Hz), indicating improved temporal alignment of brain responses over time. However, phase synchronization decreased from 6 to 12 months, suggesting a developmental transition towards more differentiated brain activity. Taken together, these findings demonstrate that auditory maturation during the first year of life follows a non-linear trajectory driven by dynamic changes in neural synchronization, reflecting the progressive refinement of functional neural circuits. Our results thus provide a critical benchmark for understanding the neural dynamics underlying sensory development during this period.

item.title: Multidimensional psycholinguistic difficulty in Cantonese picture naming: Behavioral, neural, and effective connectivity evidence.
item.description:
Brain and language
Picture naming is a useful paradigm for studying spoken word production because it requires the transformation of visual object input into a lexical response through coordinated conceptual and lexical processes. This study examined whether inherent psycholinguistic difficulty in picture naming is multidimensional or unitary. Thirty-eight healthy native Cantonese speakers performed an overt object picture-naming task during fMRI. Four psycholinguistic variables were modeled: conceptual familiarity, average neighborhood distance (AND), naming disagreement, and lexical frequency. Mixed-effects models showed that higher conceptual familiarity and lexical frequency facilitated naming, whereas higher AND increased both errors and response times; naming disagreement increased errors but did not significantly affect response times. Importantly, we observed a significant interaction between conceptual familiarity and lexical frequency on response times, indicating the facilitative effect of frequency was modulated by familiarity. For errors, significant interactions were found between conceptual familiarity and lexical frequency, as well as between AND and lexical frequency, and between AND and naming disagreement, revealing complex joint influences on naming accuracy. Whole-brain analyses revealed dissociable neural effects across variables. Conjunction analysis showed that lower conceptual familiarity and higher AND converged in bilateral lateral occipital and ventral occipitotemporal regions, with extension into the left posterior temporal cortex, suggesting shared sensitivity to semantic-level difficulty. In contrast, naming disagreement and lexical frequency did not show significant lexical-level overlap. Effective connectivity analyses further identified a stable directed ROI architecture during naming. Together, the findings support a multidimensional account of picture-naming difficulty in which semantic- and lexical-related item properties impose partially distinct but interacting constraints on spoken word production.

item.title: Spatial and functional organization of the somato-cognitive action network (SCAN) during cue and execution of motor tasks.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
The primary motor cortex has traditionally been conceptualized as a somatotopically organized structure, with discrete cortical regions corresponding to specific body parts. However, accumulating evidence suggests that motor cortex organization extends beyond simple effector-based representations to include higher-order functional systems supporting goal-directed behavior. Here, we examine the somato-cognitive action network (SCAN), a set of inter-effector cortical regions located between the classical hand, foot, and face representations of primary motor cortex that has been proposed to integrate cognitive control processes with motor function. Using task-based functional MRI during a motor paradigm that dissociates cue-related and execution-related processes, we investigated the functional role and spatial organization of SCAN in healthy adults. SCAN exhibited preferential activation during the cue phase, greater than during movement execution, indicating a prominent role in action preparation rather than motor output. In contrast, classical effector-specific motor representations corresponding to individual body parts (hand, foot, and face) showed greater engagement during execution, consistent with their role in movement generation. Across these SCAN regions, activation increased systematically from dorsomedial regions (adjacent to leg representations) to ventrolateral regions (adjacent to face representations). This spatial gradient was accompanied by progressively greater dominance of preparatory SCAN activity relative to movement-related activity in the adjacent effector regions. Together, these findings demonstrate that motor cortex organization includes a distinct integrative system that is temporally and spatially dissociable from effector-specific representations. These results support an integrate-isolate framework in which cognitive and motor processes are differentially expressed across the cortical landscape, providing new insight into the functional architecture of human motor control.

item.title: Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns of Dynamic Audiovisual Social Stimuli in Autism Spectrum Disorder (Heterogeneous Encoding Patterns in Autism).
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
The neural basis of social difficulties in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) remains uncertain. Prior studies typically used static stimuli or reduced complex stimuli to only a few dimensions, obscuring real-world complexity. Here, we used videos with social content to engage brain networks and trained encoding models to predict brain activity from high-dimensional audio, visual, and more abstract socially relevant features (e.g., valence). We hypothesized that brain activity in autistic adults would be less accurately predicted and more heterogeneous within and across individuals than in neurotypical (NT) participants, particularly for socially relevant features. Participants [48 ASD (13 female), 90 NT (25 female)] viewed six videos (5-20 min). Brain activity was measured using fMRI. Cross-validated encoding models were assessed on prediction accuracy, variance, and pattern similarity. Brain activity was predicted significantly above chance across brain networks and videos with striking consistency between groups. Auditory and language networks were most accurately predicted. Within-participant predictions were equally variable between groups; however, autistic participants exhibited lower within-group encoding pattern similarity than NT participants and greater across-group than within-group similarity. Analyses using only socially relevant features showed the largest across-group differences in encoding pattern similarity. The novel application of encoding models to multiple videos in ASD suggests greater heterogeneity in neural representations of social information in ASD. Although group-averaged encoding accuracies were comparable across groups, ASD participants showed more heterogeneous regional encoding patterns. These idiosyncratic patterns underscore the need to incorporate individual variation in brain representations when developing translational neuroimaging approaches in autism.Significance statement Individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) experience difficulties in social communication and interaction, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we present a novel application of encoding models to neuroimaging in ASD. Neural representations of dynamic and complex social information were more heterogeneous across autistic as compared with neurotypical individuals while encoding model prediction accuracy was similar for population averages across groups. Effects were robust across six videos and spatial scales. Variability in neural representation across individuals, rather than systemic population differences, may thus be associated with atypical brain function in complex social information processing in autism. The findings highlight the importance of accounting for individual variability when studying the neurobiology of autism and developing translational neuroimaging approaches.

item.title: The disrupted navigational compass: pathophysiological mechanisms and clinical interventions for spatial navigation deficits.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Spatial navigation is a higher-order integrative cognitive ability that supports environmental orientation, goal-directed route selection, and adaptive locomotion by integrating spatial memory, multisensory cues, attention, and executive control. Neural systems supporting navigation are also vulnerable to aging and neurodegenerative disease, making navigation a useful domain for linking basic mechanisms with clinically measurable functional impairment. This review summarizes spatial-navigation mechanisms across multiple levels. At the cognitive level, navigation depends on interacting processes including spatial representation, path integration, reference-frame transformation, landmark use, and route planning. At the network level, hippocampal-entorhinal, retrosplenial-parietal, scene-selective, and prefrontal systems contribute complementary functions. At the cellular level, place-, grid-, head-direction-, speed-, and boundary-related representations encode position, heading, self-motion, environmental geometry, and prospective behavior. Clinical and neuroimaging studies indicate that navigation impairment is associated with structural and functional abnormalities, with the strongest diagnostic evidence currently arising from Alzheimer's disease and its prodromal stages. VR-based behavioral assessment and electrophysiological approaches provide complementary means of characterizing navigation phenotypes: VR enables controlled, repeatable, process-sensitive tasks, whereas intracranial and scalp recordings provide neural information at different spatial and physiological scales. No pharmacological agent has been developed or licensed specifically for navigation impairment; current navigation-focused interventions therefore rely mainly on behavioral and VR-based rehabilitation, compensatory strategies, and emerging neuromodulation approaches. Future studies should integrate process-specific behavioral and physiological markers with biomarker-defined clinical cohorts, and use large, randomized, longitudinal studies to establish diagnostic validity, real-world transfer, and mechanism-informed intervention effects.

item.title: Multidimensional Neural Maturity Indices from Naturalistic fMRI Reveal the Longitudinal Development of Theory of Mind.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Theory of Mind (ToM) develops from early reasoning about others' beliefs and intentions toward more advanced forms of recursive and socially embedded mental-state understanding. This ability emerges alongside the progressive maturation of large-scale brain networks. Here, we introduce a multidimensional neural maturity framework, derived from naturalistic functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), that characterizes children's neurofunctional maturation along three dimensions: functional connectivity, temporal fluctuation, and spatial activation, by capturing neural responses to social narratives. Using an accelerated longitudinal design (baseline ages 3-9 years; 27-30-month follow-up), we applied this framework to examine how social-cognitive brain networks mature across complementary dimensions of brain function and how such maturation relates to ToM development. Across childhood, all three neural indices increased longitudinally, indicating progressive maturation of social-cognitive networks. Brain-behavior analyses further highlighted temporal fluctuation and spatial activation maturity as dimensions most closely related to ToM performance. Longitudinal path models indicated developmental continuity from elementary to advanced ToM, and suggested that advanced mental-state reasoning develops in coordination with the multidimensional longitudinal maturation of social-cognitive neural responses. Together, these findings provide initial longitudinal neurodevelopmental evidence that children's social-cognitive networks become increasingly adult-like across multiple neurofunctional dimension, offering a neurodevelopmental extension of behavioral accounts of the transition from elementary to advanced mental-state reasoning.

item.title: Associations between white matter network alterations and visuospatial and social-emotional deficits in patients with right hemisphere tumors: a prospective clinico-radiological study.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Preserving neurological function is crucial in brain tumor surgery. Because the right hemisphere supports visuospatial and social‑cognitive abilities, damage may affect quality of life. This prospective study (TANGO; ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04288505) examined associations between visuospatial and social‑emotional deficits and tractography‑based white matter alterations in patients with right hemisphere tumors. Thirty‑four patients were assessed preoperatively and 22 postoperatively using diffusion magnetic resonance imaging and four neuropsychological tests. Tractography metrics were extracted for nine right hemisphere tracts. Thirty‑four Human Connectome Project participants served as controls. Preoperatively, deficits in visuospatial functioning, facial emotion recognition, and mentalizing were associated with predominantly right hemisphere microstructural abnormalities within distributed white matter networks. Visuospatial deficits were associated with alterations involving the frontal aslant tract (FAT), arcuate fasciculus (AF), superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF), and SLF II; facial emotion recognition deficits with the SLF III and uncinate fasciculus (UF); and mentalizing deficits with the AF. Postoperatively, exploratory findings suggested associations between new social-emotional deficits and structural alterations involving the inferior longitudinal fasciculus (ILF), SLF, and SLF III, whereas new visuospatial deficits showed a trend toward reduced right FAT volume. Relative to controls, left hemisphere tractographic changes were observed regardless of the presence of visuospatial and/or social-emotional deficits, whereas right hemisphere alterations were primarily observed in patients with such deficits. These findings highlight the role of right hemisphere networks in supporting visuospatial and social-emotional functioning. Further characterization of white matter connectivity may help improve risk stratification, surgical planning, and rehabilitation strategies.

item.title: The many facets of human brain asymmetry.
item.description:
Nature reviews. Neuroscience
Asymmetry on the left-right axis is an organizing principle of the human brain that is important for diverse cognitive and behavioural functions. Advances in neuroimage analysis, genomics and large-scale data collection in the past decade have transformed our understanding of the biological foundations and multivariate nature of brain asymmetry. In this Review, we synthesize evidence across scales - from functional and macro-anatomical asymmetries and their inter-relations to microstructural, cellular and molecular levels. We examine inter-individual variation and atypical forms of brain asymmetry, which reveal that diverse aspects of asymmetry can vary largely independently across individuals rather than constituting a single trait. In this context, we discuss the developmental origins, lifespan trajectories and genetic architecture of hemispheric differences. We also summarize the relevance of brain asymmetry for neurological and psychiatric disorders and evolutionary changes of brain asymmetry that occurred in humans. Through this synthesis, we illustrate how contrasting the left and right hemispheres provides an informative window into the multi-level brain organization that supports cognition and behaviour.

item.title: Personalized Functional Network Mapping Across the Lifespan.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Functional brain networks vary substantially across individuals, yet this variability is obscured by conventional group-average atlases. Personalized functional network mapping addresses this limitation by characterizing individual-specific network organization, including the spatial topography of network territories, boundaries, and variants. Personalized mapping can be applied across large developmental and aging cohorts to study lifespan changes in such organization. Precision functional mapping (PFM), a specialized form of personalized mapping, uses extensive functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data per individual to achieve highly reliable and fine-grained characterization of individual functional organization. Here, we review individual-specific functional network organization from infancy through older adulthood. Evidence across life stages suggests a lifespan trajectory in which individual-specific network organization is detectable near birth, continues to refine through childhood and adolescence, and exhibits marked trait-like stability in adulthood, while its evolution in later life remains less well characterized. Across these stages, inter-individual topographic variability is greater in higher-order association than primary sensorimotor systems, positioning the sensorimotor-association axis as a unifying framework for understanding individual-specific network organization across the lifespan. We further review how individualized network features relate to cognition and psychopathology and how they are altered in psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. Finally, we discuss advances in MRI acquisition and analysis that facilitate personalized functional network mapping and opportunities for precision clinical translation.

item.title: Disentangling the Spatiotemporal Neural Dynamics of Conflict Detection and Resolution between Lexical and Sublexical Processes in Oral Word Reading: An Intracranial SEEG Study.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Object recognition relies on correspondence between whole objects and their subcomponents. When this correspondence is disrupted, accurate recognition requires detecting conflicts and inhibiting misleading subcomponent information, yet the neural basis underlying these processes remain unclear. Written language, with sublexical components that may conflict with whole words, provides an ideal testbed. Using stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) recorded from 39 participants (both sexes) during Chinese character reading, we revealed a functional dissociation between neural systems supporting conflict detection and inhibitory control. Conflict detection was associated with β band activity in the fusiform gyrus and widespread θ and α band effects across temporal and parietal regions. Inhibitory control was associated with α and β band activity in the inferior frontal and precentral gyri. Granger causality analysis showed increased β band connectivity from conflict-processing to inhibitory-control regions under conflict conditions. These findings demonstrate that disruptions of whole-sublexical correspondence engage dissociable neural systems for conflict detection and inhibitory control, implemented through frequency- and region-specific neural oscillations and coordinated via increased information transfer from posterior to frontal regions.Significance Statement Reading often requires resolving conflicts between competing linguistic representations, yet the neural mechanisms that detect such conflicts and resolve them remain poorly understood. Using stereo-electroencephalography with millimeter-scale spatial and millisecond-scale temporal resolution, we dissociated sublexical conflict detection from inhibitory control during Chinese character reading. We show that these processes are supported by distinct low-frequency oscillatory networks and are linked through directed functional interactions. These findings move beyond traditional accounts of sublexical effects by identifying their underlying cognitive components and neural dynamics, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding how cognitive control supports fluent word recognition.

item.title: Category learning drives cortical attentional gain to diagnostic dimensions of perceptual information.
item.description:
PLoS biology
Humans and other animals develop remarkable perceptual and cognitive specializations for identifying, differentiating, and acting on classes of ecologically important signals. This expertise is flexible enough to support diverse perceptual judgments: a voice, for example, simultaneously conveys what a talker says, as well as myriad cues about her identity and state. Expert perception across complex signals thus involves discovering and learning regularities that best inform diverse perceptual judgments, as well as weighting this information flexibly as task demands change. Here, we test whether this process may involve attentional gain. We use two prospective auditory category learning tasks to relate a complex, entirely novel soundscape to four classes of 'alien identity' and two classes of 'alien size.' Identity, but not size, categorization requires discovery and learning of patterned acoustic input situated in one of two simultaneous, non-overlapping frequency bands. This allows us to capitalize on the coarsely segregated, frequency-band-specific channels tiling auditory cortex. We use fMRI to ask whether category-relevant perceptual information present in one frequency band is prioritized relative to simultaneous, uninformative information in the other frequency band. Only among participants expert at alien identity categorization do we observe neural prioritization of the identity-diagnostic frequency band. This prioritization persists even when the diagnostic information becomes irrelevant in the size categorization task. Tellingly, the neural selectivity evoked implicitly in the identity categorization task aligns with that in an independent task, where activation is driven by explicit and sustained selective attention to pure tones in one or the other frequency band. Additionally, the learning trajectories taken to achieve expert-level categorization leave fingerprints on the patterns of neural activity associated with the diagnostic dimension. In all, this indicates that learning categories can drive attentional gain to category-diagnostic input dimensions.

item.title: Beyond sleep macrostructure: a high-definition review of acupuncture's electrophysiological signatures in modulating sleep microarchitecture (spectral power, spindles, and slow oscillations).
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Sleep science has shifted from coarse stage-based metrics toward a microstructural perspective that treats electroencephalographic biomarkers, spectral power, sleep spindles, and slow oscillations as candidate windows onto restorative brain function. This high-definition review evaluates whether acupuncture has been shown to modify these features. Direct evidence from natural overnight sleep is currently very limited: most available electrophysiological studies were conducted during quiet wakefulness, in resting daytime EEG recordings from clinical groups, or under propofol anesthesia. These studies demonstrate that acupuncture or related electrical acupoint stimulation can produce state-, region-, and frequency-dependent changes in EEG power and network organization, but they do not yet establish increased NREM spindle density, improved slow-oscillation-spindle coupling, enhanced slow-wave morphology, memory consolidation, or glymphatic clearance. We therefore distinguish directly observed findings from indirect mechanistic support and from hypotheses that require prospective testing. Plausible pathways include ascending somatosensory influences on thalamocortical excitability, autonomic and hypothalamic effects that may reduce hyperarousal, and peripheral or central neurochemical processes involving adenosine, GABA, serotonin, and BDNF; however, the causal sequence from needling to sleep microarchitecture remains unproven. Future progress requires preregistered, adequately powered, multi-night studies using validated spindle and slow-wave detectors, explicit control estimands, and multimodal measurements. Biomarker-guided and closed-loop acupuncture should presently be regarded as a research framework rather than an established treatment strategy.
